Now let me organize the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I have gathered. Here is the commentary:

## Exodus 16 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Arrival at the Wilderness of Sin

- **Traditional reading:** This marks exactly one month since leaving Egypt (they departed on the 15th of Nisan, now it is the 15th of Iyar). Israel moved from Elim (an oasis of 12 springs and 70 palm trees) toward Sinai, and in between lay the Wilderness of Sin. The name "Sin" has no connection to the English word "sin"; it is a geographical name, perhaps related to "Zin." However, as events unfold, this wilderness became a place very much associated with the sin of grumbling. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

- **Gill:** Notes from Numbers 33:10 that Israel actually camped by the Red Sea again after Elim before reaching the Wilderness of Sin — an unmentioned intermediate stop. He also notes the desert was known for vipers and lizards, truly a dangerous place. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/16.htm)

### v. 2 — The Whole Congregation Grumbles

- **Traditional reading:** The people "grumbled" against Moses and Aaron. The Hebrew word (from root *lun*) describes open rebellion, not mere dissatisfaction. This was "mutiny against Almighty God." Whereas earlier only "the people" grumbled (Ex 15:24), now "the whole congregation" does — grumbling spreads like leaven. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Spurgeon:** "They have been only about six weeks in the wilderness, and already they are up in arms against their leaders. Remember that we have the same kind of people to deal with as Moses and Aaron had." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

### v. 3 — Romanticizing Egypt

- **Traditional reading:** The people twist their memory of Egypt, speaking as if slavery was a time of feasting at "pots of meat" and "bread to the full." This is selective memory supporting their complaining. They also falsely accuse Moses of bringing them out to "kill this whole assembly with hunger." Starvation was more *anticipated* than *experienced*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

- **Gill:** Notes the exaggeration — it is unlikely that slaves in hard bondage had leisure to sit by fleshpots and eat to satiety. They also had flocks and herds with them (see v. 3), so starvation was not actually imminent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/16.htm)

- **D.A. Carson (cited at Precept Austin):** They "sarcastically romanticize their experience of slavery (!) in Egypt." The real issue is that they see God as existing to serve them. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

### v. 4 — God Promises Bread from Heaven

- **Traditional reading:** God responds to grumbling with grace, not judgment — He will "rain bread from heaven." Bread does not normally rain from heaven; this is a supernatural provision. Yet God will not drop it into their mouths; they must go out and gather. The provision comes with a "test" — will they obey instructions regarding daily gathering and the Sabbath? (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

- **Ellicott:** "Human life is a probation. God proves and tries those most whom He takes to Himself for His 'peculiar people,' and the trial is often by means of positive precepts." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

- **Lutheran (1517.org):** The LORD provides "saving bread." This manna points forward to Christ as the Bread of Life (John 6) and ultimately to the Sacrament of the Altar. (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-exodus-162-15-pentecost-10-series-b)

### v. 5 — The Sixth Day Promise

- **Traditional reading:** On the sixth day, the people would find they had gathered twice as much. This prepared for the Sabbath rest.

- **Ellicott:** Suggests this is not a command but an announcement of a fact — "You will find that what you have gathered turns out to be twice as much." A miraculous doubling is intended. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

- **Calvin:** Notes that God "so far extended His liberality as abundantly to satisfy them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/exodus-16.html)

### vv. 6–8 — Moses and Aaron Address the People

- **Traditional reading:** Moses announces that by evening they will know the LORD brought them out, and in the morning they will see His glory. This is remarkable — after the plagues, Passover, and Red Sea, they still needed to "know" this. Moses twice insists: "Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD." Even complaints against leaders are ultimately complaints against God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

- **Precept Austin (Ryken):** The word "grumbling" hardly does justice. In Hebrew it describes "an open rebellion." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

### vv. 9–10 — The Glory of the LORD Appears

- **Traditional reading:** Aaron summons the congregation to "come near before the LORD." As he speaks, the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud — likely an intensification of the pillar of cloud that already led them. The glory cloud reveals God's presence but also hides His face so the unholy are not consumed. (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-exodus-162-15-pentecost-10-series-b; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Gill:** Christ, the brightness of the Father's glory, appeared in the cloud "in some visible displays of his majesty." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/16.htm)

### vv. 11–12 — God Speaks: Meat and Bread

- **Traditional reading:** God publicly confirms what Moses already knew — at twilight they will eat meat (quail), and in the morning bread. The purpose: "Then you will know that I am the LORD your God." God's provision is revelatory; it teaches who He is. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

### v. 13 — Quail in the Evening

- **Traditional reading:** That evening quail "came up and covered the camp." These migratory birds fly across the Sinai Peninsula between southern Europe and Arabia. They are small, bullet-headed birds that roost on the ground when exhausted — making them easy to catch. This was a one-time provision at this point (unlike Numbers 11 where quail came for a month as judgment). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Gill:** Notes that these quail were an emblem of worldly things — "not the portion of the saints… not abiding, but transitory things." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/16.htm)

### vv. 14–15 — The Manna Appears / "What Is It?"

- **Traditional reading:** After the dew evaporated, "thin flakes" remained, "as fine as frost." The people asked, "What is it?" — in Hebrew *man hu*, which became the name "manna." They did not recognize God's provision because it came in an unexpected form. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Ellicott:** Disputes the translation "It is manna." The Hebrew *man hu* must be rendered either "What is this?" (LXX, Vulgate) or "This is a gift." *Man* does not mean "what" in Hebrew (only in Chaldee/Aramaic), but it can mean "gift" in Arabic; the Hebrew root *manan* means "to give." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

- **Physical description (compiled from various verses):** White like coriander seed (v. 31), the size of a sesame seed, sweet like honey wafers. Could be ground, baked, or boiled. Numbers 11:7–8 adds that it was the color of bdellium (pearly) and tasted like pastry prepared with oil. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

### vv. 16–18 — Gathering Instructions and the Miracle of Equal Measure

- **Traditional reading:** Each person was to gather an omer (about 2–3 quarts). Some gathered more, some less, but when measured "he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall." This is clearly miraculous — the manna somehow adjusted to exactly an omer per person. God provided neither too little for the weak nor too much for the greedy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

- **Spurgeon:** "God meant it to be so. Not every man according to his avarice, that he might save any of it, but 'every man according to his eating.' God took care that neither should feebleness be stinted, nor should greed have any excess." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons39/sermons39.xliv.html)

- **Ellicott:** Calls this "only… miraculous" — whatever the quantity collected, when measured in camp, the result was always exactly an omer per head. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

### vv. 19–21 — No Hoarding / Disobedience and Decay

- **Traditional reading:** Moses commanded not to keep any until morning. Some disobeyed — and it "bred worms and stank." Moses was angry. This was a test of daily trust: they were to depend on God each day, not hoard. The manna also melted when the sun grew hot, forcing an early-morning work ethic. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-16-commentary)

- **Ellicott:** Notes the corruption was a punishment for disobedience, not natural decomposition — because on the Sabbath it did not spoil (v. 24). "Neither of the natural mannas is subject to any very rapid decomposition." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

### v. 22 — Double Portion on the Sixth Day

- **Traditional reading:** On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much — two omers each. The leaders were surprised and reported it to Moses. This was the miracle God promised in v. 5. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Coffman:** Notes there were two great miracles here: first, that unequal gathering always measured equally; second, that on the sixth day each man measured out exactly double. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-16.html)

### vv. 23–26 — The Sabbath Instituted (or Re-Instituted)

- **Traditional reading:** Moses declares, "Tomorrow is a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD." The people are to bake and boil what they need on the sixth day, and the leftover will keep for the seventh without spoiling. On the Sabbath itself, no manna would appear. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Crucial denominational difference — Was the Sabbath already known or first instituted here?**

  - **Baptist / Reformed / Presbyterian (Guzik, Calvin, Spurgeon, Keil & Delitzsch):** This was the *first time* God explicitly spoke to Israel about the Sabbath. Guzik: "This was the first time God spoke to Israel about the Sabbath. God essentially forced them to honor the Sabbath." Keil & Delitzsch: "It is perfectly clear from this event, that the Israelites were not acquainted with any sabbatical observance at that time." The Sabbath was raised into a legal institution only through the Decalogue. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-16.html)

  - **Methodist / Wesleyan / Anglican (Benson, Ellicott):** The Sabbath was a *primaeval* institution dating from creation (Gen 2:2–3), already known to the patriarchs but *re-instituted* here after being lost during Egyptian bondage. Benson argues: "If the sabbath had now been first instituted, how could Moses have understood what God said to him (Ex 16:5) concerning a double portion… without making any express mention of the sabbath? And how could the people have so readily taken the hint?" Ellicott also allows: "Much, no doubt, may be said in favour of a primaeval institution of the Sabbath." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/exodus-16.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

  - **Calvin:** Takes a moderate view — "It is questionable whether it had already been observed by the patriarchs. It appears probable that it was; but I am unwilling to make it a matter of contention." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/exodus-16.html)

  - **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "And yet the Sabbath had not been instituted according to the Law of God, which proves that its foundation lay deeper and earlier than the promulgation of the Ten Commandments! It is bound up with the essential arrangement of time since the creation." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons39/sermons39.xliv.html)

- **Lutheran (1517.org):** The glory cloud presence "makes clear who is providing this meal." The emphasis is on God's provision and presence, with the cloud both revealing and hiding His glory. No specific Lutheran distinctive on the Sabbath timing was found in the sources. (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-exodus-162-15-pentecost-10-series-b)

### vv. 27–29 — Sabbath Violators

- **Traditional reading:** Some went out on the seventh day anyway — and found nothing. God rebukes them: "How long will you refuse to keep My commandments?" The LORD had *given* them the Sabbath as a gift, not a burden. "Everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Ellicott:** Explains "abide ye every man in his place" — some Jews took this literally and stayed frozen in position all Sabbath. But the general understanding was that it forbade leaving the *camp*. Hence the later concept of a "Sabbath day's journey" (traditionally about six stadia, the distance from the camp centre to its boundary). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

### v. 30 — The People Rest

- **Traditional reading:** "So the people rested on the seventh day." Brief but significant: they finally obeyed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

### v. 31 — Manna Described

- **Traditional reading:** "The house of Israel called the bread manna" (meaning "What is it?"). It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. God gave them good-tasting food, not tasteless gruel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Jewish tradition (Ginzberg, cited in Guzik):** Legends said manna tasted like whatever the eater desired — milk for children, bread for youths, honey for the old, barley with oil and honey for the sick. But it was bitter to Gentiles. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

- **Ellicott:** In Numbers 11:8 the taste is "fresh oil." The Book of Wisdom (Wisdom 16:20–21) claims the taste "tempered itself to every man's liking." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

### vv. 32–34 — A Memorial Omer Preserved

- **Traditional reading:** God commands that an omer of manna be preserved "for the generations to come" as a testimony. Aaron places it in a jar "before the LORD" — later specified as "in front of the Testimony," meaning the Ark of the Covenant. Hebrews 9:4 confirms the ark contained the pot of manna, Aaron's rod, and the stone tablets. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

- **Ellicott:** Notes this passage "must belong to a later date than any other part of Exodus, since it assumes that the Tabernacle is set up (Exodus 16:34)." The writer placed it here to conclude the manna history. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

- **Gill:** The manna being placed "before the LORD" typifies Christ, the true bread, who is "hidden" with God until revealed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/16.htm)

### v. 35 — Forty Years of Manna

- **Traditional reading:** Israel ate manna for the full forty years of wilderness wandering, until they reached the border of Canaan. Joshua 5:10–12 records that it ceased the day after they ate the produce of the land. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)

### v. 36 — The Omer Defined

- **Traditional reading:** An omer is one-tenth of an ephah — perhaps 2–3 quarts. This parenthetical note was useful for later readers unfamiliar with the measure. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

---

## Summary of Protestant Differences

**The Sabbath Question (vv. 23–26).** The major exegetical divide is whether the Sabbath was *instituted* here for the first time or *re-instituted* from an earlier creation ordinance:

- **Reformed/Baptist/Keil:** The text shows Israel had no prior Sabbath knowledge; it was new to them. The Sabbath was formalized later in the Decalogue.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan/Anglican (Benson, Ellicott):** The Sabbath was known from creation (Gen 2:2–3) but had been lost during Egyptian slavery. Ex 16 *revived* it. The people's ready understanding of the double-portion hint (v. 22) before Moses explained it, and Moses' own understanding (v. 5), suggest prior knowledge.
- **Spurgeon** uniquely holds both: the Sabbath was not yet "instituted according to the Law" (Mosaic), yet its foundation was "deeper and earlier" in creation.
- **Calvin** demurs: unwilling to make the timing "a matter of contention."

---

## Other Views and Traditions

### Christological / Typological Reading (shared across traditions)

Manna is universally read as a type of Christ. Jesus Himself makes the connection in John 6:32–33: "Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but My Father gives you the true bread from heaven." The reception of manna — aware of need, daily, humbly, personally — becomes a pattern for receiving Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/)

### Lutheran Sacramental Reading

The 1517.org article explicitly ties the manna to the Eucharist (Sacrament of the Altar): "He is the saving bread from Heaven, and of course, the bread of life that is Christ's body in the Sacrament of the Altar. All of this saving bread finds its culmination in the marriage feast of the Lamb." (https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-exodus-162-15-pentecost-10-series-b)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No results were available from the permitted Catholic/Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) within the search and fetch limits. However, the manna–Eucharist typology is a standard Catholic reading, rooted in John 6 and reinforced by the manna being preserved "before the Testimony" (paralleling the reserved Sacrament). The Book of Wisdom (Wisdom 16:20–21, in the Catholic/Orthodox canon) adds that manna "tempered itself to every man's liking," a passage not in Protestant Bibles.

### Modern Scholarly Notes

No results were available from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the search/fetch limits.

### Manna and Natural Explanations

Guzik notes some identify manna with a natural substance produced by tamarisk trees in the Sinai today — insects puncture the bark, excrete a sugary globule that melts in the sun. However, the biblical manna differs decisively: it appeared in vast quantities year-round for 40 years, ceased on the Sabbath, and behaved miraculously (spoiling or not spoiling according to God's command). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-16/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/16.htm)
